common_name: Thai Green Eggplant (Small Striped Round Eggplant for Curry)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55F. Thai Green thrives in Gulf South heat and humidity, continuing to produce through the hottest part of summer.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest young at golf-ball to small-egg size for the crisp, mild, low-seed texture prized in Thai cooking. Thai Green is a small, round eggplant with pale to medium green skin lightly streaked with cream, borne in heavy clusters on compact, productive plants that thrive in hot, humid conditions. The firm, dense flesh holds its shape well when simmered whole or halved directly into Thai green curry, a traditional use where the small green fruit is added along with pea eggplants and other aromatics. Its heat tolerance and continuous production over a long summer season make it an excellent, prolific choice for Gulf South vegetable gardens.

common_name: Painted Serpent Cucumber (Striped Light-and-Dark Green Armenian Cucumber)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Painted Serpent is a striped heirloom Armenian cucumber (botanically a muskmelon) with alternating light and dark green ribbing along its long, curved fruit.

directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile, moist soil in full sun; provide a trellis for the straightest fruit shape and harvest at 12-18 inches for the best texture. Painted Serpent bears the same extraordinarily long, curling fruit typical of Armenian cucumber, but distinguished by striking alternating stripes of light and dark green running the length of the fruit, an eye-catching heirloom pattern that sets it apart in the garden and at market. Like other Armenian cucumbers it is botanically a muskmelon rather than a true cucumber, giving it notably better heat tolerance through Gulf Coast summers than standard cucumbers, with thin, edible skin and mild, non-bitter, faintly melon-scented flesh. Harvest regularly to keep vines productive, since old, oversized fruit develops tougher skin and more prominent seeds.
